genZNote: Rides the exact same tick as Lyme disease — which is why co-infection is a real thing your doctor actually checks for.

morphology.shape: Intraerythrocytic ring forms and characteristic tetrads ('Maltese cross')
morphology.size: Ring forms ~1-3 µm within red blood cells

lifeCycleStages: Gametocyte (ingested by tick, sexual cycle in tick gut)

habitat.naturalHabitat: Red blood cells of infected mammals; maintained in nature via a rodent (white-footed mouse)-tick cycle
habitat.hostAssociation: Reservoir hosts are small rodents, especially the white-footed mouse; Ixodes scapularis ticks serve as the vector
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Endemic to the northeastern and upper midwestern United States, overlapping with Lyme disease-endemic regions
habitat.reservoir: White-footed mice and other small rodents

microscopy.appearance: Intraerythrocytic ring forms resembling Plasmodium falciparum, but classically forming tetrads ('Maltese cross') and lacking hemozoin pigment
microscopy.arrangement: Rings and tetrads within red blood cells

culture.growthCharacteristics: Diagnosis relies on blood smear, serology, and PCR rather than culture

biochemicalTests.result: Highly sensitive, useful especially with low parasitemia
Useful adjunct, particularly for past or low-level infection

identificationClues: Intraerythrocytic ring forms on Giemsa-stained blood smear, resembling Plasmodium falciparum
Characteristic tetrad ('Maltese cross') formation and absence of hemozoin pigment help distinguish it from Plasmodium
History of tick exposure in an endemic area (northeastern/upper midwestern US), sometimes with concurrent Lyme disease symptoms
More severe disease in asplenic, elderly, or otherwise immunocompromised patients

diseases: Babesiosis — fever, fatigue, and hemolytic anemia; ranges from asymptomatic/mild in healthy hosts to severe, life-threatening illness in asplenic, elderly, or immunocompromised patients
virulenceFactors: Intraerythrocytic replication causing direct red cell lysis and hemolytic anemia
Asplenic patients lose a key mechanism for clearing infected/damaged red blood cells, greatly increasing disease severity
clinicalImportance.transmission: Bite of an infected Ixodes scapularis tick (the same tick species that transmits Lyme disease and Anaplasma, making co-infection a recognized clinical concern); rarely via blood transfusion or congenitally
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Endemic to the northeastern and upper midwestern United States, geographically overlapping with Lyme disease; clinicians should consider co-infection with Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum in patients with a tick bite from an endemic area
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Because ring forms resemble Plasmodium falciparum on blood smear, travel/exposure history (tick vs. malaria-endemic travel) is essential to guide the correct diagnosis; PCR is more sensitive than smear for low-level parasitemia

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — diagnosed by blood smear/PCR/serology
examFacts.importantDisease: Babesiosis — fever and hemolytic anemia, severe in asplenic/elderly patients
examFacts.importantTest: Giemsa blood smear (Maltese cross tetrads); PCR
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: An intraerythrocytic parasite transmitted by the same Ixodes tick as Lyme disease, forming distinctive Maltese-cross tetrads without the pigment seen in Plasmodium
